title: Patrick Dougherty: How to Build AI Agents that Actually Work

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's central object is the agent system—its definition, ACI design, model-selection strategy, multi-agent manager-worker patterns, and harness architecture rather than any single tool or workflow engine. Lessons are cross-domain and applicable to any agent build, while the audience and tooling context (building without frameworks/SDKs) aligns with developer platforms. Content spans designing agent architecture, iteratively building and testing ACI, and addressing production concerns like framework dependency and credential cascading. Assumes familiarity with LLM tool calling, RAG, and SQL schemas but remains accessible to practitioners without deep ML or systems expertise. summary: Patrick Dougherty recounts rebuilding Rosco's product around AI agents starting two years ago, before frameworks or SDKs existed. He defines an AI agent by three criteria: it must take directions toward a specific objective, have access to at least one tool with responses, and autonomously reason about when and how to use tools, excluding predefined prompt-chained sequences. A core lesson is enabling the agent to think rather than stuffing knowledge into the system prompt via RAG; instead, they used discrete retrieval tool calls. For SQL generation, flooding the prompt with all tables and columns overwhelms the model, so they broke retrieval into iterative building blocks: search tables, get table detail, and profile a column. He contrasts GPT-4o, which produces SQL even when the task is impossible, with o1, which correctly reasons that churn cannot be calculated from a given Salesforce schema. He emphasizes the Agent Computer Interface (ACI)—the exact syntax and structure of tool calls and responses—where trivial-seeming tweaks yield large gains. JSON worked best for GPT-4o, XML for Claude. He treats the model as the agent's brain, preferring Claude 3.5 for the decision-making layer due to its balance of speed, cost, and judgment. Fine-tuning was deemed a waste of time because it overfits and degrades reasoning. On frameworks, they avoided abstractions like LangGraph because production requirements such as cascading end-user security credentials into the agent were difficult with third-party tools; frameworks are useful for prototyping but risky for production dependency. He argues the agent itself is not a moat—the ecosystem around it, including user experience, connections, and security protocols, constitutes the real value and is the most time-consuming part of building production-quality agents. For multi-agent systems, he recommends a hierarchical manager-worker structure where the manager owns the final outcome and delegates subtasks to worker agents with more specific context and tools. He applies a two-pizza rule limiting teams to 5-8 agents, noting that systems with 25-50 agents strongly decrease the likelihood of accomplishing the outcome due to infinite loops or unrecoverable paths. He stresses incentivizing the manager agent with the overall objective rather than forcing worker agents through discrete steps. He references a blog post at asb.com with further multi-agent design principles.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: An AI agent must take directions, access at least one tool, and autonomously reason about tool use—not follow predefined prompt chains.
Prioritize enabling the agent to reason via discrete retrieval tool calls rather than injecting knowledge into the system prompt via RAG.

Avoid over-relying on frameworks for production agents due to blockers like user-credential cascading and authentication management.

sections.title: Introduction and AI Agent Definition
sections.summary: Patrick introduces himself as co-founder and CTO of Rosco, which rebuilt its product around AI agents two years ago. He defines an AI agent by three criteria: taking directions toward a specific objective, having access to at least one tool with responses, and autonomously reasoning about how and when to use tools, excluding predefined prompt-chained sequences.

sections.title: Reasoning Over Knowledge: Retrieval Tool Calls and SQL Example
sections.summary: He explains the lesson of focusing on enabling the agent to think rather than limiting it to the model's inherent knowledge. Instead of RAG inserting content into the system prompt, they used discrete retrieval tool calls. He illustrates with SQL generation: providing all tables and columns overwhelms the model, so they built iterative tools like search tables, get table detail, and profile a column. He contrasts GPT-4o (writes SQL even when impossible) with o1 (reasons that a churn query is unanswerable from the given Salesforce schema).

sections.title: Agent Computer Interface (ACI) Iteration
sections.summary: He introduces ACI—the exact syntax and structure of tool calls and responses—and stresses that small, seemingly trivial tweaks yield large performance gains. Examples include switching GPT-4o responses from markdown to JSON to fix column blindness in long search results (customers had 500-1000 column tables, ~30,000 token responses), while Claude preferred XML. He advises treating the model as the agent's brain and using a generally intelligent model like Claude 3.5 for decision-making.

sections.title: Hallucinations, Fine-Tuning, and Frameworks
sections.summary: He explains that observing hallucination patterns reveals the model's expected tool-call formats, which you should match to improve performance. Fine-tuning was a waste of time—it overfits and degrades reasoning. On frameworks, they avoided abstractions because none existed when they started and because production needs like cascading end-user Snowflake OAuth credentials into the agent were difficult with frameworks like LangGraph. He recommends frameworks for prototyping but warns against production dependency.

sections.title: Agent Moat and Multi-Agent Systems
sections.summary: He argues the agent itself is not a moat; the ecosystem around it—user experience, connections, and security protocols—is the real value and most time-consuming part of production. For multi-agent systems, he recommends a hierarchical manager-worker structure where the manager owns the outcome and delegates subtasks to specialized workers. He applies a two-pizza rule of 5-8 agents, noting that 25-50 agent systems risk infinite loops and failure. He stresses incentivizing the manager agent with the overall objective rather than forcing worker agents through discrete steps, and references his blog at asb.com for further detail.

demonstrations: GPT-4o given a simplified Salesforce schema (accounts, contacts, opportunities) and asked to write a churn query—produced a flawed SQL query assuming account type changes indicate churn.
o1 given the same schema and question—correctly reasoned that churn status cannot be determined from the provided schema.
Switching GPT-4o tool responses from markdown to JSON immediately resolved the agent's blindness to columns in long search results.
Claude performed better with XML-formatted tool responses rather than JSON or markdown.
limitations: Flooding the prompt with full table schemas and all columns overwhelms the model, causing wrong table selection or non-executable queries.
GPT-4o is incentivized to produce output even when a task is impossible, leading to incorrect SQL.
GPT-4o with markdown-formatted search results was sometimes completely blind to columns present in the response payload.
Fine-tuned models overfit to specific task sequences and can reduce reasoning ability.
Third-party frameworks like LangGraph made cascading end-user security credentials and authentication management difficult to scale in production.
Giving a single agent all information and tool calls overwhelms it, leading to bad decisions and bad paths.
Multi-agent systems with 25-50 agents risk infinite loops and failure to accomplish the outcome.
quantitativeClaims: Some customers had 500 or 1,000 column tables in their data warehouse.
Tool responses could reach approximately 30,000 tokens.
